newsitem.title: USA: U.S. agriculture chief sees tough resistance to biotech.
newsitem.headline: U.S. agriculture chief sees tough resistance to biotech.

text.p: Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said Friday that resistance by consumers in Europe and some other nations to genetically modified crops is much stronger than he had thought, and that he is concerned this could affect the fight against world hunger.

Speaking in a telephone news conference after the World Food Summit in Rome, Glickman said the whole area of biotechnology was extremely controversial in Europe, and that public fears were being exploited.
"I come back from the conference recognizing that these problems are more challenging than certainly I went over there thinking they were," said Glickman.

European consumers have been in an uproar in recent weeks over the marketing of a new genetically modified soybean grown in the United States this year. The soybean, developed by St. Louis-based Monsanto Co., is resistant to the Roundup pesticide, and a small amount was grown commercially by American farmers this year.

In a separate news conference in Rome, Glickman rejected a charge by environmentalists that the U.S. government was too close to big business and urged consumers not to be swayed by "rhetoric and emotion" in the dispute over the soybeans.

Protesters led by the Greenpeace group have been trying to keep the soybeans out of Europe and have chained themselves to gates in Germany, occupied the office of the Austrian health minister and climbed to the roof of the headquarters of Swiss food group Nestle SA.

"It is an issue that is very easily whipped up with rhetoric and emotion, and it is incumbent on all leaders to educate people on what the facts are and make sure science is objective," he told reporters at the food summit.
"Saying that does not mean we have all the answers or that in a supine or blind way we follow industry," he said.
Glickman noted that most cancer drugs were based on similar science that produced the soybeans.
Greenpeace said Friday that U.S. grain giant Cargill took out an injunction banning it from interfering with the arrival this weekend of another load of genetically modified soybeans.

Greenpeace said it faced fines of 1 million francs ($30,000) an hour if it comes within about half a mile of the grain ship Stanislaw Kulczynski, which is due to arrive in the Belgian port of Antwerp over the weekend.

In the teleconference with reporters in Washington, Glickman said there was currently "a lot of hostility to science," and that some circles were trying to exploit public fears "about things in the food supply that people don't know about, can't control and think is going to hurt them."
He said this was especially troubling given the challenges the world faces in feeding a rapidly growing population that he said would grow by 2.5 billion people in the next 20 years.

"How are we going to feed the world without new technology other than tearing up highly erodible soil, or tearing up the rain forests, or otherwise destroying the environment? There is no way to have it both ways," Glickman said.

Recognizing that opposition to the new soybeans appears to be strongest in Germany, Glickman said he met with Germany's minister of agriculture on the issue. He said the German official supports biotechnology but believes that the modified soybeans should be labelled "under practical circumstances."

Glickman reiterated that he was not sure that labelling of gene modified products such as soybeans can ever be done on a practical basis, but that consumers need to be educated as to the safety and real benefits of the new products.
